messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Ravi, a 26-year-old South Asian male, has been an editor for three years. His life took a dramatic turn when he witnessed a police shooting that left a colleague critically injured. Since then, Ravi’s daily routine and personal relationships have been deeply affected by the lingering trauma of this event. The day of the incident was hot, and as the police arrived, they frantically tried to subdue his colleague in front of everyone at the office. The heat from the summer sun combined with the fear-induced adrenaline made Ravi feel an intense physical discomfort that he now associates with danger. This tactile trigger—a specific temperature on his skin—leads him to withdraw into himself, feeling overwhelmed by a sense that he cannot cope with the world around him. Whenever Ravi is alone with women, a common occurrence given his editorial work often involves meetings and interactions in small office spaces, he becomes anxious and feels increasingly detached. This female presence triggers a dissociative response where he begins to feel unreal and disconnected from reality. Each time this happens, it reinforces his belief that he is a lousy coper, exacerbating the negative appraisals he holds about himself. Ravi’s memories of the event are vivid and painful. When he recalls the incident, he feels an overwhelming sense of grief that sometimes brings him to tears at work. The smell of coffee from the office machine can suddenly transport him back to the moment when his colleague was on the ground, surrounded by a mixture of fear and despair. These olfactory triggers not only evoke intense emotional reactions but also confirm for Ravi that he is incapable of handling such traumatic memories. The bodily reenactment of the event, where he feels as if he’s reliving the exact physical sensations from that day, makes it difficult for him to concentrate on his work. The combination of these memory intrusions and the resulting negative appraisals has left Ravi feeling like nothing in his life holds meaning anymore. He often wonders how he can go on when every reminder of the past seems to confirm that bad things will continue to happen. Ravi’s marriage is also strained by his condition. His wife, though supportive, finds it challenging to understand why simple interactions or even a change in temperature can trigger such profound distress. The cumulative effect of these triggers and memories has led Ravi to believe that nothing good can ever happen to him again, further isolating him from the world. Over time, these triggers and negative appraisals have formed a vicious cycle that continues to tighten around Ravi. His belief that he is a lousy coper exacerbates his fear of being alone with women or experiencing certain temperatures, which in turn makes it harder for him to cope when memories flood back. Each time this happens, the grief and despair deepen, reinforcing his negative beliefs about himself and the future. Ravi's work has suffered as well; he often misses deadlines and finds it difficult to engage fully in meetings, which are crucial for his job. His colleagues have noticed a change in him but do not understand what is happening underneath the surface. The cumulative impact of these symptoms and the reinforcing cycle they create have made Ravi realize that he needs help. What brings Ravi to therapy is not just the overwhelming nature of his symptoms but also the realization that without intervention, his life could continue to spiral downward. He is most afraid of losing control completely and feeling like a burden on his wife. At the same time, he hopes for a chance to reclaim some sense of meaning in his life and regain confidence in his ability to cope with challenges. Ravi's journey towards healing begins now, as he seeks support to break this cycle and find ways to reintegrate into his daily life without being constantly haunted by the past.
